corrections.compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 (official LLVM release tarball; the clang_cpp container aliases g++ to clang++ and links the system libstdc++, no -stdlib=libc++) and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu build), -std=c++20, glibc malloc. Headline 'prod' build (cpp/Makefile CXXFLAGS_PROD): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections (not -O3). The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -fvisibility=hidden -fno-trapping-math) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use or -fprofile-use) variants of every C and C++ benchmark; the Makefile passes -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) only at the link step while the objects are compiled without -flto, so those builds probably get no LTO (inference from cpp/Makefile). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO configurations were compared here (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Managed side: Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 run as 'java -Xmx2g -jar' (default G1 GC, C2 JIT), GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1 (JDK 25.0.4.1.1) with -Xmx2g, dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1 (Release), Julia 1.13.1 with --threads=16 (versions and run commands from the results file).
corrections.why_faster: Standard-library and allocator differences, not JIT codegen (from the sources): C++ tokenizes with std::istringstream operator>> (sentry, locale-aware whitespace skipping and per-character stream extraction into a std::string) and builds a fresh std::unordered_map<std::string,int> each iteration, one malloc'd node per distinct word, freed at the end of run(); Java uses String.split(" "), which takes a non-regex fast path for a one-character delimiter, and a HashMap whose String, node and Integer objects are bump-allocated and reclaimed by the young-generation GC. AOT-compiled C#/AOT (1.399 s), Rust (0.898-1.001 s), Crystal (0.88 s) and Zig (0.57-0.91 s) also beat every C++ row, so the gap reflects the C++ iostream-based tokenizer rather than a JIT advantage.
corrections.caveats: The win comes from the C++ tokenizer and per-node hash-map allocation, not from JIT compilation: C#/AOT and the AOT languages Rust, Crystal and Zig also beat every C++ row, so the 'runtime-jit-beats-aot' framing does not fit; a std::string_view split loop in C++ would likely change the result (inference, not measured). Both versions do the same work (whitespace split, hash count, max scan) over 50,000 words of 3-8 letters (all within libstdc++'s small-string buffer), 360 timed iterations. The C version (strdup of the whole text every iteration, strtok_r, uthash with strdup'd keys) is slower still at 1.963-2.084 s. Memory trade: Java/OpenJDK RSS 309 MB vs C++ 7.5-7.9 MB. Margin is modest (1.25x over the best C++ row, C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s) and rests on one run per configuration, although all 16 C/C++ configurations land between 1.587 and 2.042 s. LangArena's own README calls it 'a subjective benchmark', and the author says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. benchmarks.rb runs each test once per configuration in its own process and records that single in-process timing (no repeats, no variance). Every language, C and C++ included, runs a warm-up of 20% of the iterations before the timer starts, so JIT compilation and startup are excluded. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3, PGO and fast-math variants were also measured and still lose on this test; the Makefile's LTO flags are link-only, so no configuration had real LTO. Rows were selected by the search agent as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most other tests in the suite go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and the Binarytrees::Arena variant). The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.

notes: Numbers verified exactly (Java/OpenJDK 1.272 s, Java/GraalVM/JIT 1.15 s, C#/JIT 1.422 s, C++/G++ 1.638 s, C++/G++/Fast 1.651 s, C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s best, Julia 1.857 s). Shortcomings: the win is a standard-library effect (istringstream tokenizer plus node-per-key unordered_map against String.split and a GC'd HashMap), AOT C#, Rust, Crystal and Zig also beat C++, so the category label 'runtime-jit-beats-aot' misattributes it; single run per configuration; 40x more memory on the JVM; the Makefile's LTO flags are link-only.

HotSpot allocates the short-lived TreeNode objects by pointer bump in thread-local allocation buffers and reclaims them with G1's generational collector, whose cost scales with live data; the harness's final System.gc() runs after the timer stops. Every C/C++ flag set except the instrumented C/Gcc/PGO/Gen build lands at 2.08-2.55 s, so the cost is malloc/free, not codegen. .NET (also a GC'd JIT) takes 4.27-4.51 s, so the win is specific to HotSpot's allocator and GC. The suite's index-based Binarytrees::Arena variant reverses the result (C/Gcc/Fast 0.255 s vs Java/OpenJDK 1.086 s).

The C++ timed region includes freeing each tree, while the JVM's last collection (System.gc() after the timer) is not timed; young collections during the run are timed. corrections.why_faster: From the sources: the timed test is parsing only, so there is no node dispatch or evaluation. Java allocates the same nodes by pointer bump, and the dead ASTs of earlier iterations cost G1's young collections almost nothing because collection cost scales with live data; the harness's final System.gc() runs after the timer. JavaScript on Bun and Deno also beats every C++ row, which points to allocation and deallocation cost rather than JIT codegen.
